tips.title: Halve it: the pulse goes there and back
tips.body: $\text{distance} = \dfrac{v t}{2}$. Forgetting the ÷ 2 gives an answer exactly **twice** the truth, and it is the commonest error in the topic. Given the distance instead, you **double** it to find the time.

tips.title: S for solid
tips.body: **S-waves are transverse and travel through solids only**; **P-waves are longitudinal and cross both solids and liquids**. One letter carries the whole distinction, and the S-wave shadow is what proved the outer core is liquid.

tips.title: Ultrasound is about frequency, not loudness
tips.body: It is sound **above the upper limit of human hearing**, about 20 000 Hz. *Very loud sound* and *very fast sound* both score nothing — the definition is entirely about **frequency**.

tips.title: Partially reflected is the useful word
tips.body: Some reflects and **some carries on**, so one pulse returns echoes from several depths. That is why an image can be built at all, and *partially* is usually a mark in its own right.

tips.title: What fails to arrive is evidence
tips.body: The outer core was shown to be liquid by S-waves **not** arriving. If a question asks what a shadow zone shows, the reasoning is always: this wave cannot travel through that material, so that material must be there.

why.matters:
You cannot see a baby before it is born, the seabed under a ship, or the inside of the Earth. This topic is one trick used three ways: send a wave in, and read what comes back. Where it reflects tells you where a boundary is, how fast it travelled tells you what it passed through, and where it fails to arrive tells you what was in the way.

Every echo sum in it is the same sum, and every one has the same trap: the time measured is there and back.

examples.title: Why the sonographer squirts gel on first
examples.body:
An ultrasound scan works because ultrasound is **partially reflected at a boundary** between two materials. Skin to muscle, muscle to fluid, fluid to the baby: each boundary sends a little back, and the time for each echo, at about 1 540 m/s in tissue, gives its depth.

The one boundary that must not be there is skin to air. At that one almost the whole pulse reflects straight back off the surface and nothing gets in, which is why the probe is pressed into a layer of gel: it fills the gap, so the first boundary the pulse meets is the skin itself.

examples.title: The parking sensor
examples.body:
The beeps that quicken as a car reverses towards a wall are an echo sounder in the bumper. It sends out a pulse of ultrasound, times the echo, and works out the gap with the topic's one equation: distance is speed times time, **halved** because the pulse went there and back.

At 340 m/s in air, an echo after 6 ms puts the wall about 1.0 m away; 3 ms is 0.51 m; 1.5 ms is 0.26 m and the tone goes solid. Forget the halving and the sensor would let you reverse into the wall at what it thought was a metre.

props.title: In air at 340 m/s, there and back

visual.alt: A table of a parking sensor's echo times, six milliseconds for about a metre, three for half a metre and one and a half for a quarter, each halved because the pulse travels there and back

examples.title: Why a phone can warn of an earthquake before it arrives
examples.body:
An earthquake sends out both kinds of seismic wave at once. **P-waves** are faster, about 6 km/s through the crust; **S-waves**, the ones that do most of the shaking, travel at about 3.5 km/s. The further you are from the quake, the further the two pull apart.

A sensor near the quake feels the P-wave and sends a message at the speed of light. 100 km away the P-wave arrives after about 17 s and the S-wave after about 29 s: 12 seconds to get under a table. It is the topic's own idea, that different waves travel at different speeds through the same rock, turned into a warning.

props.title: P-waves at 6 km/s, S-waves at 3.5 km/s

visual.alt: A table showing that at fifty, one hundred and two hundred kilometres from an earthquake the faster P-wave arrives six, twelve and twenty four seconds before the S-wave, which is the warning time

steps.title: Seeing what cannot be seen
steps.body:
This topic is **physics only** and **Higher tier only**.

The idea behind all of it is one sentence from the specification: **differences in velocity, absorption and reflection between different types of wave in solids and liquids can be used to detect and explore structures hidden from direct observation.**

Unpack that and it says something simple. When a wave meets a **boundary between two different materials**, part of it is **reflected**. If you know how fast the wave travels and you measure **how long the reflection takes to come back**, you can work out **how far away that boundary is** — without ever seeing it.

And because different waves behave differently in different materials — some pass through liquids, some do not; some are absorbed, some are not — what does and does not come back tells you **what the hidden material is**, not only where it is.

Three applications are named, and they are the same idea at three scales:

- **Ultrasound**, for medical and industrial imaging
- **Echo sounding**, for the depth of water and objects in it
- **Seismic waves**, for the structure of the Earth itself

the depth of water and objects in it

steps.title: Ultrasound
steps.body:
**Ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans** — above about **20 000 Hz**. That is the definition, and it is worth stating that way rather than as *very high frequency sound*.

The property that makes ultrasound useful:

**Ultrasound waves are partially reflected when they meet a boundary between two different media.**

**Partially** is the important word. Some of the wave reflects and some carries on — which is exactly what is needed, because the part that carries on can reflect again from a **deeper** boundary. One pulse can therefore return several echoes, one from each boundary it meets.

**How a distance is found.** The time taken for the reflections to reach a detector is measured. Since the speed of the wave in the material is known, and the pulse has travelled **to the boundary and back**:

$$\text{distance to the boundary} = \frac{\text{speed} \times \text{time}}{2}$$

The **÷ 2** is the whole difficulty of the calculation, and leaving it out doubles the answer.

**Used for:** medical imaging, including scans in pregnancy, and **industrial imaging** — finding cracks and flaws inside metal castings, where a flaw is a boundary between metal and air and so reflects strongly.

**Echo sounding uses high frequency sound waves to detect objects in deep water and to measure water depth.** It is the same calculation as ultrasound, at a larger scale.

steps.title: Seismic waves
steps.body:
**Seismic waves are produced by earthquakes**, and they come in two kinds whose different behaviour is what revealed the inside of the Earth.

**P-waves** are **longitudinal** seismic waves. They **travel at different speeds through solids and liquids** — and, crucially, they **can travel through both**.

**S-waves** are **transverse** seismic waves. **S-waves cannot travel through a liquid.**

That single difference does the work. A transverse wave needs the material to resist being sheared sideways, and a liquid cannot — it simply flows. A longitudinal wave only needs the material to be squashed and stretched, which a liquid can do.

**What this revealed.** After an earthquake, detectors around the world record what arrives. They find:

- a large region on the far side of the Earth where **no S-waves arrive at all**
- P-waves that arrive, but **refracted** — their paths bent, because their speed changes as they pass through different materials

The S-wave shadow can only be explained if the waves have passed into something they cannot travel through — so **part of the Earth's core is liquid**. And the way the P-waves bend gives the **size** of that region.

**P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure and size of the Earth's core.**

The spec also asks you to be aware of the wider point: **the study of seismic waves provided new evidence that led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.** Nobody has ever been to the core. Everything known about it is inferred from waves that have been through it.

steps.title: Why the differences matter
steps.body:
The spec's framing is about **velocity, absorption and reflection**, and each of the three does a different job.

**Reflection** tells you **where** a boundary is. A wave partially reflects at the boundary between two different materials, and the time for the echo gives the distance. This is the basis of ultrasound and echo sounding.

**Velocity** tells you **what** the material is. A wave's speed depends on the material it is travelling through, so a change of speed marks a change of material — and it is why P-waves **refract** inside the Earth, bending as they cross between regions. Tracking those bends maps the regions.

**Absorption** tells you what a wave can and cannot get through. A wave that is strongly absorbed will not reach a detector, so its **absence** is itself information — which is exactly how the S-wave shadow works, though there the cause is that S-waves cannot propagate in a liquid at all.

That is the general lesson of the topic, and worth stating in an answer: **what fails to arrive is evidence too.** The discovery that the outer core is liquid came not from something detected but from something that was expected and was **missing**.

steps.title: Going deeper: the factor of two, and absence as evidence
steps.body:
**The halving.** Every echo calculation in this topic has the same trap. The measured time is for the **round trip**, so:

$$\text{distance} = \frac{v t}{2}$$

Forgetting the ÷ 2 gives an answer exactly **twice** the true distance, and it is the single most common error. A quick check: does your answer make sense? A seabed 60 m down when the echo took 0.04 s is plausible; a **baby** 20 cm deep in an ultrasound scan is not.

The reverse also appears: given the distance, the time is $t = \dfrac{2d}{v}$ — doubled, not halved. Work out which journey the time refers to before rearranging anything.

**Why partial reflection matters.** If a boundary reflected **all** the ultrasound, nothing would travel deeper and you would learn about the first boundary only. Because reflection is **partial**, the remainder continues, reflects from the next boundary, and returns later. A single pulse therefore produces a **series of echoes at different times**, each from a different depth — and that series is what builds an image rather than a single measurement.

**Absence as evidence.** The S-wave shadow is a good example of something worth being able to articulate: the discovery was of something **not arriving**. Detectors across a large region recorded no S-waves at all after an earthquake. Since S-waves are **transverse** and a liquid cannot support a transverse wave — it flows rather than resisting the sideways shear — the only explanation is that they met **liquid** on the way. That is how we know the outer core is liquid, and nobody has ever been near it.

The P-waves add the other half. They **do** get through, but **refract** as their speed changes between materials. The pattern of where they emerge gives the **size** of the region.

**Being precise about definitions.**

- **Ultrasound** is sound **above the upper limit of human hearing**, about 20 000 Hz. Not *very loud sound*, not *any high sound*.
- **P-waves are longitudinal, S-waves are transverse.** If you can only hold one, remember that **S** cannot cross a liquid — **S for solid**.
- Seismic waves come from **earthquakes**, not from equipment.

questions.prompt: A ship uses echo sounding to measure the depth of water. Explain how the method works, and calculate the depth if the echo returns after 0.06 s in water where sound travels at 1500 m/s.
questions.solution: A pulse of high frequency sound is sent downwards from the ship into the water. When the pulse reaches the seabed it meets a boundary between two different media, the water and the seabed, and part of the pulse is reflected back upwards. A detector on the ship receives this reflection and the time taken between sending the pulse and receiving the echo is measured. Because the speed of sound in sea water is known, the total distance travelled by the pulse can be calculated from distance equals speed multiplied by time. In this case that is one thousand five hundred multiplied by nought point zero six, which gives ninety metres. However, this is the distance for the whole journey, because the pulse has travelled down to the seabed and then back up again to the ship. The depth of the water is therefore half of this total, which is forty five metres. The same method can be used to detect objects in deep water, such as a shoal of fish or a wreck, because an echo returning sooner than expected shows that something is reflecting the pulse above the seabed.

questions.modelAnswer:
**How it works.**

1. A pulse of **high frequency sound** is sent downwards from the ship.
2. At the **seabed** it meets a **boundary between two different media**, and part of it is **reflected**.
3. A **detector** on the ship receives the echo, and the **time** between sending and receiving is measured.

**The calculation.** The speed of sound in sea water is known, so

$$\text{total distance} = v t = 1500 \times 0.06 = 90 \text{ m}$$

But that is the **whole journey** — down **and back up**. So

$$\text{depth} = \frac{90}{2} = \mathbf{45 \text{ m}}$$

**The extension.** The same method finds **objects in deep water**: an echo returning **sooner** than the seabed's shows something reflecting the pulse above it — a shoal of fish, or a wreck.

The halving is the mark this question exists to test. Answering 90 m puts the seabed twice as deep as it is.

questions.prompt: Explain how the behaviour of P-waves and S-waves provides evidence for the structure and size of the Earth's core.
questions.solution: An earthquake produces two types of seismic wave, P-waves which are longitudinal and S-waves which are transverse. Detectors placed around the surface of the Earth record which waves arrive at each place and at what time. It is found that over a large region on the far side of the Earth from the earthquake no S-waves arrive at all, a region known as the S-wave shadow. S-waves are transverse waves, and a transverse wave cannot travel through a liquid because a liquid cannot resist being sheared sideways and simply flows instead. The fact that the S-waves do not arrive can therefore only be explained if they have encountered liquid material on their way through the Earth, which provides the evidence that part of the Earth's core is liquid. P-waves, being longitudinal, are able to travel through both solids and liquids, but they travel at different speeds in different materials, so their paths are refracted as they pass from one region of the Earth into another. By recording where the P-waves emerge at the surface and working back along their refracted paths, the size of the liquid region can be determined. In this way the structure and the size of the Earth's core have been worked out from waves alone, even though no part of the core has ever been directly observed.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The two waves.** An earthquake produces **P-waves**, which are **longitudinal**, and **S-waves**, which are **transverse**.

**The observation.** Detectors around the Earth record what arrives where. Over a large region on the far side, **no S-waves arrive at all** — the S-wave shadow.

**The physics.** S-waves are **transverse**, and a transverse wave **cannot travel through a liquid**: a liquid cannot resist being sheared sideways, it simply flows.

**The conclusion.** The only explanation for their absence is that the S-waves met **liquid** on the way. So **part of the Earth's core is liquid**.

**The size.** P-waves are longitudinal and **do** get through, but they travel at **different speeds in different materials**, so their paths **refract** at each boundary. Recording where they emerge and working back along those paths gives the **size** of the liquid region.

The wider point the specification asks for: all of this concerns a part of the Earth **nobody has ever observed directly**. The evidence came from waves — and in the S-wave case, from waves that **failed to arrive**.

examTechnique.body:
Decide first whether the time given is for the journey there, or there and back. Almost always it is the round trip, so halve the distance.

Define ultrasound by frequency, above the upper limit of human hearing, not by loudness.

Say partially reflected when describing what happens at a boundary, and say why that matters for imaging.

For seismic waves, name the type of each wave before saying what it can travel through. The conclusion follows from the type.

When explaining the S-wave shadow, state the observation, then the property of transverse waves, then the conclusion, in that order.

Check a calculated distance is physically sensible before writing it down.
examinerErrors: Forgetting to divide by two, so every distance is doubled.
Halving when the distance is given and the time is wanted, instead of doubling.
Defining ultrasound as very loud sound.
Saying ultrasound is completely reflected at a boundary.
Saying P-waves cannot travel through a liquid, which reverses the conclusion.
Saying seismic waves are produced by equipment rather than earthquakes.
Stating that the core is liquid without giving the S-wave evidence for it.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer works out which journey the measured time refers to before touching the equation, so it halves and doubles in the right places. It defines ultrasound by frequency and explains why **partial** reflection is what makes imaging possible. On seismic waves it builds the argument in order — the observation, the property of transverse waves, then the conclusion — rather than asserting that the core is liquid. And it can state the wider point: that the evidence came from waves failing to arrive, about a place nobody has ever seen.
